A.explanation: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium, measured vertically on the $d$ axis, not a time interval on the $t$ axis.

B.explanation: Frequency is $f = 1/T$ and is not read directly as a distance; the $t$ axis interval between repeating points gives the time for one oscillation first.

C.explanation: X to Y is the time for one complete oscillation from one descending zero to the next identical point, which is the period $T$.

D.explanation: Wavelength is a distance in space from a displacement-distance graph, but this graph is displacement-time for one point so the horizontal axis is time.

hints: Notice the axes: the vertical axis is displacement $d$ and the horizontal axis is time $t$ for one fixed point on the string.
Look at X and Y on the $d$-$t$ curve: both are at $d = 0$ with the curve falling through zero, so the motion repeats identically at Y as at X.
Recall what time interval is measured between two successive identical phases on a $d$-$t$ graph, and how it relates to $f = 1/T$ and to wavelength.
walkthrough: Identify the graph type: variation of displacement $d$ with time $t$ for a single point, so any horizontal distance is a time interval, not a length along the string.
Locate X and Y: X is where the curve crosses $d = 0$ going downwards after one crest, and Y is the next place where it crosses $d = 0$ going downwards after the following crest.
State the rule: the period $T$ is the time for one complete oscillation, meaning the time to return to the same displacement moving in the same direction.
Check the interval: between X and Y the point completes one trough, one return to zero, one crest and a return to descending zero, which is exactly one full cycle.
Exclude the other quantities: amplitude is the peak $d$ value, wavelength needs a displacement-distance graph, and frequency must be calculated from $f = 1/T$.
Therefore the $t$ distance from X to Y represents the period. This is option C
